interest: Reconstructs Japan's hidden 1940 gold and balance-of-payments data, and debates blocking Japanese bond sales in Iloilo.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.51, spanning late January to late February 1940) centers on Japanese international financial resources, gold movements, and bond transactions during the Second Sino-Japanese War. The primary document is an extensive, strictly confidential State Department study prepared by economic specialist George F. Luthringer and transmitted by Herbert Feis, analyzing Japan's dwindling gold reserves, newly mined and reclaimed domestic gold production, foreign exchange holdings, and balance of payments deficits with non-yen-bloc countries at the close of 1939. The remainder of the file documents a legal and diplomatic controversy in the Philippine Islands: the interception at the port of Iloilo of Japanese Government national defense bonds imported to solicit defense funds from local Japanese residents, prompting inter-agency coordination between U.S. High Commissioner Francis B. Sayre, the State Department, and Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Jerome N. Frank to determine whether such transactions could be halted under the Securities Act of 1933 given that the Neutrality Act of 1939 had not been invoked.

subfiles.about: Transmittal of George F. Luthringer's report on Japanese gold and foreign exchange resources at the end of 1939 to Far Eastern and political advisers.
subfiles.summary: Feis forwards Luthringer's study of Japanese utilizable foreign assets at end-1939 to Hamilton and Hornbeck, noting no clear evidence of major drawdowns besides gold, though Feis would be surprised if assets were untouched; data remains insufficient for certainty.
subfiles.title: Transmittal Memorandum from Herbert Feis to Maxwell M. Hamilton and Stanley K. Hornbeck Regarding Japanese Utilizable Foreign Assets
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton and Stanley K. Hornbeck

subfiles.about: A detailed economic intelligence report assessing Japanese official gold reserves, gold production and acquisition, foreign exchange resources, and non-yen-bloc trade balances at the end of 1939.
subfiles.summary: This comprehensive strictly confidential report prepared by George F. Luthringer examines Japan's dwindling gold and foreign exchange position at the close of 1939 in the face of a complete Japanese statistical blackout. Luthringer estimates remaining official gold reserves at $153,000,000 (including $38,000,000 in transit to the United States and $115,000,000 in the Bank of Japan), reflecting an estimated net decrease of $99,000,000 over 1939 following $171,000,000 in gold exports against approximately $84,000,000 in newly mined and requisitioned domestic gold. The study notes that the Bank of Japan has likely drawn upon its legal reserve and maintains its published ¥501,000,000 reserve figure only by unofficially marking holdings to current depreciated market exchange rates. While Japan's trade deficit with non-yen-bloc nations narrowed, high gold exports were sustained by foreign suppliers demanding cash in advance for critical goods such as machine tools ahead of the expiration of the U.S.-Japan commercial treaty. Luthringer concludes that Japan's remaining gold reserves could be depleted by mid-1941, though approximately $200,000,000 in secondary international assets might sustain external purchasing power for up to three years. Page 22 represents a trailing microfilm resolution target card.
subfiles.title: Report on Japanese Gold and Foreign Exchange Resources at the End of 1939

subfiles.about: Reporting the arrival of eight Japanese Government bonds at the port of Iloilo and raising the question of the applicability of the Neutrality Act of 1939.
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 37: High Commissioner Sayre reports eight Japanese Government bonds (¥1,450) imported at Iloilo to collect defense contributions from Japanese residents; since no belligerency was proclaimed, the Neutrality Act did not bar entry, and Sayre seeks State's concurrence.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 37 from High Commissioner Francis B. Sayre Regarding Importation of Japanese Government Bonds at Iloilo

subfiles.about: Requesting the Securities and Exchange Commission's opinion on the applicability of the Securities Act of 1933 to the sale of Japanese Government bonds in the Philippines.
keywords: Philippine Securities and Exchange Act of 1936
subfiles.summary: Grady sends SEC Chairman Frank Sayre's cable on the Iloilo bonds, noting State found the Neutrality Act inapplicable but had customs deny entry pending an SEC ruling, and asks whether federal securities registration law applies despite the Philippines' own 1936 Securities Act.
subfiles.title: Letter from Assistant Secretary of State Henry F. Grady to SEC Chairman Jerome N. Frank Regarding Sale of Japanese Bonds in the Philippines

subfiles.about: Instructing the U.S. High Commissioner in the Philippines to advise customs to refuse entry to Japanese Government bonds pending SEC determination.
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 32: Hull tells Sayre the Neutrality Act doesn't bar the Iloilo bond entry absent a neutrality proclamation, but customs should refuse entry while the SEC decides if the Securities Act of 1933 applies.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 32 to High Commissioner Sayre Advising Suspension of Japanese Bond Entry Pending SEC Determination
